Sharpen Without Search: On-Policy Distillation of Sequence-Level Power Distribution

Erfan Baghaei Potraghloo ††thanks: Corresponding author: baghaeip@usc.edu.    Seyedarmin Azizi    Arya Fayyazi Affiliation: University of Southern California, Los Angeles, USA    Saeid Shokoufa Affiliation: University of Southern California, Los Angeles, USA    Mehdi Kamal Affiliation: University of Southern California, Los Angeles, USA    Souvik Kundu Affiliation: Intel AI, USA†\dagger Equal contribution authors.    Massoud Pedram Affiliation: University of Southern California, Los Angeles, USA
Abstract

A language model can give a correct answer more probability than any single incorrect answer and still usually sample an incorrect one, because the incorrect answers together hold more probability. The power distribution raises each complete answer’s probability to a power above one and renormalizes, shifting probability toward answers the model finds most likely (sharpening). Sampling from it improves reasoning without changing parameters, but needs many scored candidates per query. We show that a model can instead be trained to produce such answers in one generation. On-policy power distillation (oppd) runs a sequential Monte Carlo sampler in which the model being trained generates candidates and a frozen teacher’s power distribution weights them; the same probabilities weight each answer in a maximum-likelihood update. Training raises single-generation accuracy by up to 23.023.0 points on MATH500 and 27.327.3 on GSM8K over the untrained model at the same temperature, and one generation scores 2.42.4 and 3.53.5 points above published power sampling with 6464 candidates, recovering 94%94\% of the gain that 1616 candidates give the untrained model. For context, against GRPO trained with verified rewards from the same checkpoint and budget, oppd scores 3.83.8, 4.04.0 and 5.45.4 points higher on MATH500, GSM8K and AIME using no reference answers; the two are complementary, and oppd applied after GRPO adds up to 9.39.3 points. Trained only on mathematics, oppd raises HumanEval accuracy by up to 5.35.3 points. One loss coefficient moves the sharpening exponent the model absorbs between 1.191.19 and 2.022.02, against 1.141.14 for ordinary on-policy distillation, and it rises mostly on the model’s own answers. Gains hold across model families and sizes, including a model already trained with verified rewards, where lowering the temperature gives nothing and oppd adds 4.44.4 points on MATH500. Code: https://github.com/ArminAzizi98/OPPD.

1 Introduction

Let pp be an autoregressive language model that assigns probability p⁡(y∣x)=∏tp⁡(yt∣x,y<t)p(y\mid x)=\prod_{t}p(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t}) to an answer yy given a prompt xx, where the prefix y<ty_{<t} denotes the tokens before position tt. Sampling from pp can return an incorrect answer even when the correct answer is more probable than any single incorrect one, because the incorrect answers together hold more probability. The power distribution with exponent α≥1\alpha\geq 1,

πα​(y∣x)=p​(y∣x)αZα​(x),Zα​(x)=∑y′p​(y′∣x)α,\pi_{\alpha}(y\mid x)=\frac{p(y\mid x)^{\alpha}}{Z_{\alpha}(x)},\qquad Z_{\alpha}(x)=\textstyle\sum_{y^{\prime}}p(y^{\prime}\mid x)^{\alpha}, (1)

where Zα​(x)Z_{\alpha}(x) is the normalizing constant, moves probability toward the most probable answers, an effect we call sharpening. Under πα\pi_{\alpha}, the ratio between the probabilities of two answers is their ratio under pp raised to the power α\alpha. Drawing samples from πα\pi_{\alpha} instead of from pp raises reasoning accuracy by amounts comparable to reinforcement-learning post-training, without changing any parameter (Karan & Du, 2026; Ji et al., 2026). On 250250 MATH500 problems, Qwen2.5-Math-7B scores 66.8%66.8\% when it generates one answer and 79.2%79.2\% when a sampler with sixteen candidates draws approximate samples from πα\pi_{\alpha}. This sampler, however, has to run again for every query.

In this paper we ask whether this cost can be paid once, during training. Ordinary distillation trains a student to match a teacher’s next-token probabilities. The next-token probabilities of πα\pi_{\alpha}, however, depend on all possible continuations of the prefix, so no teacher forward pass computes them. Samples from πα\pi_{\alpha} can therefore only be drawn approximately, by a sampler run at inference time. Our method, on-policy power distillation (oppd), trains the student on the output of such a sampler, the sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) sampler of Azizi et al. (2026). This sampler extends NN candidate answers in blocks of tokens and gives each candidate an importance weight, which measures how much more probable it is under πα\pi_{\alpha} than under the distribution that generated it. When these weights become too uneven, it replaces low-weight candidates with copies of high-weight ones. In oppd the student generates the candidates and a frozen teacher defines πα\pi_{\alpha}; in self-distillation, the teacher is a copy of the initial student. The teacher probabilities that set the importance weights also give each complete answer a training weight, and the student is updated by weighted maximum likelihood on its own answers (Figure 1). A second loss term, the token-level anchor with coefficient λ\lambda, keeps the student’s next-token distributions near those of the teacher at temperature 1/α1/\alpha.

Contributions.

(1) A training method that uses no reference answers, verifier or reward model, in which one teacher forward pass per block of tokens supplies both the importance weights and the training weights. (2) A trained model that replaces the sampler, scoring above published power sampling with 6464 candidates on the same model and obtaining 94%94\% of the gain that sixteen candidates give the untrained model. (3) A reference point for the size of this gain. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) trains on verified rewards computed from reference answers, so it uses information oppd never reads. Trained from the same checkpoint for the same number of steps, oppd scores higher on MATH500, GSM8K and AIME, and we trace the difference to training groups in which every sampled answer receives the same reward and GRPO gets no learning signal. Applied after GRPO, oppd improves the model further, so the two are complementary. We are not proposing oppd as a replacement for reinforcement learning from verified rewards, and we compare against one standard implementation at one budget rather than against that literature. (4) A measurement of how much sharpening the student absorbs, as an exponent fitted between the student’s token probabilities and those of its initialization (Section 4). This exponent decreases monotonically as λ\lambda increases and rises mainly on the answers the student writes itself. A quantity measured before training predicts the best λ\lambda for each model.

2 Background

2.1 Sharpening complete answers versus sharpening tokens

Lowering the sampling temperature is cheaper and may appear to have the same effect, but the two operations differ. Sampling at temperature τ\tau is token-level: it replaces each next-token distribution by one proportional to its probabilities raised to the power 1/τ1/\tau, renormalizing at every position. The power distribution is sequence-level: (1) renormalizes once, over complete answers. Temperature therefore compares next tokens without information about the answers they lead to, while the power distribution gives little total probability to answers that begin with a prefix whose continuations are all uncertain. In the two-token example of Appendix A, the power distribution at α=2\alpha=2 places 0.2130.213 on answers beginning with the uncertain token and temperature 1/21/2 places 0.3080.308 there.

2.2 Drawing samples from the power distribution

The constant ZαZ_{\alpha} in (1) sums over every possible answer and cannot be computed, so samples from πα\pi_{\alpha} are drawn approximately with sequential Monte Carlo (Doucet et al., 2001; Del Moral, 2004; Del Moral et al., 2006). The sampler extends NN candidate answers in parallel, which the SMC literature calls particles. The next token of each candidate is drawn from a proposal distribution qtq_{t}, any distribution that depends only on the prompt and the prefix. With pTp_{\mathrm{T}} the model whose power distribution is sampled (the teacher in oppd), each candidate carries an importance weight, the product of the incremental importance weights

ωt=pT​(yt∣x,y<t)αqt​(yt∣x,y<t),\omega_{t}=\frac{p_{\mathrm{T}}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})^{\alpha}}{q_{t}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}, (2)

over its tokens so far. Candidate ii thus has importance weight W~t(i)=∏s≤tωs(i)\tilde{W}^{(i)}_{t}=\prod_{s\leq t}\omega^{(i)}_{s} after tt tokens. Rescaling these weights to sum to one gives the normalized importance weights W(i)W^{(i)}. The effective sample size, ESS=(∑i(W(i))2)−1\mathrm{ESS}=(\sum_{i}(W^{(i)})^{2})^{-1}, approximates the number of candidates with non-negligible weight: it equals NN when all weights are equal and 11 when one candidate holds all of the weight. When the ESS falls below a threshold, the sampler resamples the candidates: it discards low-weight candidates, duplicates high-weight ones and resets all weights to be equal. Resampling moves computation toward high-weight prefixes while the answers are still being written (Appendix F).

The effective sample size measures a divergence.

The Rényi divergence of order β\beta between distributions PP and QQ is

Dβ(P∥Q)=1β−1log∑yP(y)βQ(y)1−β,β>0,β≠1,D_{\beta}(P\|Q)\;=\;\frac{1}{\beta-1}\,\log\sum_{y}P(y)^{\beta}\,Q(y)^{1-\beta},\qquad\beta>0,\;\beta\neq 1, (3)

with β=1\beta=1 defined by continuity as the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence (Rényi, 1961). Let qq be the proposal probability of a complete answer and w=πα/qw=\pi_{\alpha}/q, its importance weight divided by ZαZ_{\alpha}. Then 𝔼q​[w]=1\mathbb{E}_{q}[w]=1 and 𝔼q[w2]=eD2(πα∥q)\mathbb{E}_{q}[w^{2}]=e^{D_{2}(\pi_{\alpha}\|q)}, so for large NN

ESS/N≈𝔼q[w]2/𝔼q[w2]=e−D2(πα∥q).\mathrm{ESS}/N\;\approx\;\mathbb{E}_{q}[w]^{2}/\mathbb{E}_{q}[w^{2}]\;=\;e^{-D_{2}(\pi_{\alpha}\|q)}. (4)

The ESS measured while the sampler runs therefore estimates a divergence between πα\pi_{\alpha} and the proposal distribution, which we use in Section 5.3.

Theorem 1 (Best proposal distribution that depends only on the prefix).

Consider all proposal distributions that are positive wherever pTp_{\mathrm{T}} is. The unique choice that minimizes the conditional variance of the incremental importance weight (2) is to sample from the teacher at temperature 1/α1/\alpha, that is qt⋆​(v)∝pT​(v∣x,y<t)αq^{\star}_{t}(v)\propto p_{\mathrm{T}}(v\mid x,y_{<t})^{\alpha}. Under this choice ωt\omega_{t} equals Zt=∑upT​(u∣x,y<t)αZ_{t}=\sum_{u}p_{\mathrm{T}}(u\mid x,y_{<t})^{\alpha} whatever token is drawn.

This is the locally optimal proposal distribution of Doucet et al. (2000), written for the power distribution; the proof is in Appendix C. The Rényi entropy Hα​(p)=11−α​log​∑vp​(v)αH_{\alpha}(p)=\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\log\sum_{v}p(v)^{\alpha} is small when pp is concentrated, and logZt=(1−α)Hα(pT(⋅∣x,y<t))\log Z_{t}=(1-\alpha)H_{\alpha}(p_{\mathrm{T}}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})), so summing over positions gives the log importance weight of an answer under q⋆q^{\star},

logW~=(1−α)∑tHα(pT(⋅∣x,y<t)),\log\tilde{W}=(1-\alpha)\textstyle\sum_{t}H_{\alpha}\!\left(p_{\mathrm{T}}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\right), (5)

which is non-positive because α>1\alpha>1. A candidate therefore keeps its weight when the teacher was confident at every position of its answer and loses weight where the teacher was uncertain. This is the sampler’s only selection rule, and it uses only the teacher’s output probabilities.

As usual in SMC, the sampler does not estimate the twist function Vt=∑y>tpT(y>t∣y1:t)αV_{t}=\sum_{y_{>t}}p_{\mathrm{T}}(y_{>t}\mid y_{1:t})^{\alpha}, on which the next-token distribution of πα\pi_{\alpha} depends. Weighting and resampling correct for it.

3 Method

We want the student pϕp_{\phi}, with parameters ϕ\phi, to minimize Dβ(πα∥pϕ)D_{\beta}(\pi_{\alpha}\|p_{\phi}) for some β>0\beta>0. Because ZαZ_{\alpha} cannot be computed, πα\pi_{\alpha} can be neither evaluated nor sampled exactly, and the gradient of the divergence has both problems. Section 3.1 rewrites the gradient to avoid both, and Sections 3.2–3.4 supply the samples, the proposal and the loss, following steps (1) to (4) of Figure 1b.

3.1 What the gradient requires

Theorem 2 (Gradient of the Rényi divergence).

For every β>0\beta>0, ∇ϕDβ(πα∥pϕ)=−𝔼π¯(β)[∇ϕlogpϕ(y)]\nabla_{\phi}D_{\beta}(\pi_{\alpha}\|p_{\phi})=-\,\mathbb{E}_{\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)}}\!\left[\nabla_{\phi}\log p_{\phi}(y)\right], where π¯(β)∝pTα​β​pϕ 1−β\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)}\propto p_{\mathrm{T}}^{\alpha\beta}\,p_{\phi}^{\,1-\beta}.

The factor 1β−1\tfrac{1}{\beta-1} in (3) cancels the factor (1−β)(1-\beta) from the chain rule for every β\beta, and ZαZ_{\alpha}, which does not depend on ϕ\phi, drops out of the gradient although it appears in the objective (Appendix C). One estimator therefore serves every β\beta, which makes β\beta a free parameter. In practice, answers can be drawn from any qq positive wherever π¯(β)\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)} is, weighted by π¯(β)​(y)/q​(y)\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)}(y)/q(y), and used in weighted maximum likelihood, the estimator of reweighted wake-sleep (Bornschein & Bengio, 2015) and of Markovian score climbing (Naesseth et al., 2020) applied here to the Rényi family. Holding the weights constant during differentiation is exact, since the derivation accounts for how π¯(β)\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)} depends on ϕ\phi (Appendices H and O).

3.2 Where the answers come from

The weight π¯(β)​(y)/q⁡(y)∝pT​(y)α​β​pϕ​(y)1−β/q⁡(y)\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)}(y)/q(y)\propto p_{\mathrm{T}}(y)^{\alpha\beta}p_{\phi}(y)^{1-\beta}/q(y) needs three numbers at every token: the teacher’s log⁡pT​(yt)\log p_{\mathrm{T}}(y_{t}), the student’s log⁡pϕ​(yt)\log p_{\phi}(y_{t}) and the proposal’s log⁡qt​(yt)\log q_{t}(y_{t}). When the student is the proposal distribution, the sampler of Section 2.2 already computes all three: (2) requires log⁡pT​(yt)\log p_{\mathrm{T}}(y_{t}) and log⁡qt​(yt)\log q_{t}(y_{t}), and the student computes log⁡pϕ​(yt)\log p_{\phi}(y_{t}) while generating the token. This choice adds no model evaluations, and one teacher forward pass per block supplies both the importance weights that decide resampling and the weights of Theorem 2 (step (4) of Figure 1b). Because the weighted answers are its own, the student is trained on the prefixes its own errors lead to (Kim & Rush, 2016; Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024).

3.3 Choosing the proposal temperature

The proposal distribution can be the student as it stands, qt=pϕq_{t}=p_{\phi}, or the student at temperature 1/α1/\alpha, qt∝pϕαq_{t}\propto p_{\phi}^{\alpha}. With qt=pϕq_{t}=p_{\phi},

log⁡ωt=α⁡(log⁡pT​(yt)−log⁡pϕ​(yt))⏟teacher–student difference+(α−1)​log⁡pϕ​(yt)⏟student’s log-probability of its own draw.\log\omega_{t}=\underbrace{\alpha\!\left(\log p_{\mathrm{T}}(y_{t})-\log p_{\phi}(y_{t})\right)}_{\text{teacher--student difference}}\;+\;\underbrace{(\alpha-1)\log p_{\phi}(y_{t})}_{\text{student's log-probability of its own draw}}. (6)

Only the first term carries information useful for training. The second depends only on which token the student happened to sample, so its distribution is the same for good and bad answers. Its standard deviation is 4.64.6 nats (natural-log units) per token at α=4\alpha=4. Over a block of Δ=64\Delta=64 tokens, the log importance weights of two candidates then differ by about 4.6​64≈374.6\sqrt{64}\approx 37 nats for reasons unrelated to their content. One candidate then receives all of the normalized weight, and the measured ESS/N\mathrm{ESS}/N stays at 1/N=0.06251/N=0.0625 from the first block onward (Appendix N). The proposal qt∝pϕαq_{t}\propto p_{\phi}^{\alpha} is the variance-optimal choice of Theorem 1 with the student in place of the teacher, and with it log⁡qt​(yt)=α​log⁡pϕ​(yt)−log⁡Ztϕ\log q_{t}(y_{t})=\alpha\log p_{\phi}(y_{t})-\log Z^{\phi}_{t} with Ztϕ=∑upϕ​(u∣x,y<t)αZ^{\phi}_{t}=\sum_{u}p_{\phi}(u\mid x,y_{<t})^{\alpha}, and log⁡ωt=α⁡(log⁡pT​(yt)−log⁡pϕ​(yt))+log⁡Ztϕ\log\omega_{t}=\alpha(\log p_{\mathrm{T}}(y_{t})-\log p_{\phi}(y_{t}))+\log Z^{\phi}_{t}. The second term of (6) disappears, and log⁡Ztϕ\log Z^{\phi}_{t} depends on the prefix but not on the token drawn, so it adds no sampling noise. With this proposal, the measured ESS/N\mathrm{ESS}/N during training lies between 0.390.39 and 0.640.64 for every model we train.

3.4 The loss

Theorem 2 averages over π¯(β)\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)}, but the candidates are drawn from qq. Self-normalized importance sampling corrects for this mismatch by assigning candidate ii the training weight

A~(i)=π¯(β)​(y(i))q⁡(y(i)),A¯(i)=A~(i)∑j=1NA~(j),∑i=1NA¯(i)=1.\tilde{A}^{(i)}\;=\;\frac{\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)}\big(y^{(i)}\big)}{q\big(y^{(i)}\big)},\qquad\bar{A}^{(i)}\;=\;\frac{\tilde{A}^{(i)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\tilde{A}^{(j)}},\qquad\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bar{A}^{(i)}=1. (7)

Both π¯(β)\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)} and qq factor over tokens, and their products over hundreds of tokens underflow, so we accumulate the logarithm one token at a time:

logA~(i)=∑t[αβlogpT(yt(i)∣⋅)+(1−β)logpϕ(yt(i)∣⋅)−logqt(yt(i)∣⋅)],\log\tilde{A}^{(i)}=\sum_{t}\Big[\alpha\beta\log p_{\mathrm{T}}(y^{(i)}_{t}\mid\cdot)+(1-\beta)\log p_{\phi}(y^{(i)}_{t}\mid\cdot)-\log q_{t}(y^{(i)}_{t}\mid\cdot)\Big], (8)

where each term is conditioned on xx and y<t(i)y^{(i)}_{<t}, and pϕp_{\phi} is the value recorded when the token was drawn. Any constant common to all candidates cancels in the normalization. The training weight is distinct from the importance weight of (2), which decides when the sampler resamples the candidates. Their per-token increments agree at β=1\beta=1, but the sum in (8) restarts at each block boundary while the importance weight accumulates from the start of the answer.

Replacing the expectation in Theorem 2 by the weighted average over the NN candidates gives a consistent gradient estimate with bias of order 1/N1/N. Holding A¯(i)\bar{A}^{(i)} fixed during differentiation makes the estimate the gradient of a loss, and dividing the loss by the mean answer length T¯=1N​∑iTi\bar{T}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}T_{i} keeps its scale independent of answer length (Appendix H). Writing πT(α)∝pTα\pi^{(\alpha)}_{\mathrm{T}}\propto p_{\mathrm{T}}^{\alpha} for the teacher’s next-token distribution at temperature 1/α1/\alpha, the objective is

ℒ⁡(ϕ)=−1T¯∑i[A¯(i)]sg∑tlogpϕ(y(i)t∣x,y(i)<t)⏟sequence-level term+λ​1T¯​N∑i,tKL(π(α)T∥pϕ)⏟token-level anchor,\mathcal{L}(\phi)=\underbrace{-\frac{1}{\bar{T}}\sum_{i}\big[\bar{A}^{(i)}\big]_{\mathrm{sg}}\sum_{t}\log p_{\phi}\!\left(y^{(i)}_{t}\mid x,y^{(i)}_{<t}\right)}_{\text{sequence-level term}}\;+\;\lambda\,\underbrace{\frac{1}{\bar{T}N}\sum_{i,t}\mathrm{KL}\!\left(\pi^{(\alpha)}_{\mathrm{T}}\,\|\,p_{\phi}\right)}_{\text{token-level anchor}}, (9)

where [⋅]sg[\cdot]_{\mathrm{sg}} is held fixed during differentiation and both KL arguments are conditioned on xx and y<t(i)y^{(i)}_{<t}.

The sequence-level term is the core of the method: its optimum is πα\pi_{\alpha}, it is the only term that uses information about complete answers, and it is the only term left when λ=0\lambda=0. The token-level anchor does not follow from Theorem 2 and moves the attainable optimum toward the teacher at temperature 1/α1/\alpha, the token-level sharpening of Section 2.1. We include it because this forward KL is mass-covering: it penalizes the student for giving little probability to tokens that πT(α)\pi^{(\alpha)}_{\mathrm{T}} considers likely. It therefore resists the concentration of all probability onto one answer, a failure we observe on models whose outputs already have little diversity. The coefficient λ\lambda trades closeness to πα\pi_{\alpha} against this protection (Section 5.3). The training weights multiply a log-likelihood rather than a divergence, because a weighted token-level divergence cannot reach πα\pi_{\alpha} (Appendix G).

3.5 Implementation

The student generates N=16N=16 candidates at temperature 1/α1/\alpha in blocks of Δ=64\Delta=64 tokens. The teacher scores all N​ΔN\Delta new tokens of a block in one forward pass, which reduces the sequential teacher calls for a TT-token answer from TT to T/ΔT/\Delta. Three details affect correctness: the importance and training weights use separate accumulators; recorded training weights are renormalized after every resampling step, so that duplicated candidates are not counted more than once (Appendix Q); and finished candidates are charged the mean per-token decrease in log importance weight of unfinished ones, so that stopping early does not raise a candidate’s weight (Appendix P).

4 Measuring absorbed sharpening

Higher accuracy alone does not show that the student moved toward πα\pi_{\alpha}, so we test a consequence that is specific to this movement. Let pbasep_{\mathrm{base}} be the model the student was initialized from, and let a context cc be a prompt with a prefix. If training sharpened the student relative to pbasep_{\mathrm{base}} with some exponent aa, so that pϕ≈pbasea/Zp_{\phi}\approx p_{\mathrm{base}}^{\,a}/Z, then

log⁡pϕ​(v∣c)=a​log⁡pbase​(v∣c)−log⁡Z⁡(c),\log p_{\phi}(v\mid c)=a\,\log p_{\mathrm{base}}(v\mid c)-\log Z(c), (10)

which is a line of slope aa in log⁡pbase​(v∣c)\log p_{\mathrm{base}}(v\mid c) at each context cc. A slope of 11 means that no sharpening was absorbed, and a slope of α\alpha means that the student equals pbasep_{\mathrm{base}} at temperature 1/α1/\alpha. We estimate the slope by least squares of log⁡pϕ\log p_{\phi} on log⁡pbase\log p_{\mathrm{base}} over the 200200 tokens most likely under pbasep_{\mathrm{base}}, weighted by pbase​(v∣c)p_{\mathrm{base}}(v\mid c) so that the near-zero tail does not dominate. We report the median slope across contexts as the absorbed exponent αeff​(pbase→pϕ)\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(p_{\mathrm{base}}\to p_{\phi}). In self-distillation αeff​(pbase→pT)=1.000\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(p_{\mathrm{base}}\to p_{\mathrm{T}})=1.000 exactly, so no measured increase can come from copying a sharper model; with a larger teacher, the control is ordinary on-policy distillation against the same teacher. The slope is dominated by noise when pbasep_{\mathrm{base}} is close to deterministic, so we report αeff\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}} only where the entropy of pbasep_{\mathrm{base}} is large enough for the fit to separate the models, and a direct entropy measurement elsewhere. Appendix M gives both and validates the estimator on synthetic logits.

5 Experiments

Setup.

Our main experiments use Qwen2.5-Math-7B (Yang et al., 2024) in self-distillation, which makes the control of Section 4 exact. We repeat the training on Qwen3-8B-Base (Yang et al., 2025), Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Qwen3-14B-Base and deepseek-math-7b-rl (Shao et al., 2024), and use Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B as the student for the sweep over λ\lambda. Training prompts are GSM8K questions (Cobbe et al., 2021) except in Appendix B.12, and no reference answer is used in training. We set α=4\alpha=4, increased linearly from 11 over the first 20%20\% of steps, with N=16N=16 candidates, blocks of Δ=64\Delta=64 tokens, resampling when the ESS falls below N/2N/2, and β=0.7\beta=0.7. Training runs for 300300 steps at two prompts per step (Appendix J). We generate four answers per problem for 200200 problems each from GSM8K and MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2024), graded with the reference power-sampling implementation. We do the same for AIME 20242024 and 20252025 pooled (6060 problems, 35003500-token limit; 40964096 for Qwen3-14B-Base). pass@1 is the fraction of the four answers that are correct, averaged over problems, and best-of-4 counts a problem solved if any answer is correct. The paired standard error on a pass@1 difference is about 2.92.9 points. Our baseline is ordinary on-policy distillation against the teacher at temperature 1/α1/\alpha, which is (9) with the anchor alone and no training weights or resampling. Our measurements of the untrained model are within 33 points of published numbers, in both directions (Appendix K). Qwen2.5-Math-7B improves under many training signals, including rewards uncorrelated with correctness (Shao et al., 2025), so the replications on other families in Section 5.4 carry as much of the claim as this model does.

5.1 Accuracy

Generating one answer at temperature 1/α1/\alpha, the model trained with oppd scores 2.42.4 points above published power sampling with 6464 candidates on MATH500 and 3.53.5 points above it on GSM8K (Table 1). Two further seeds score 79.5079.50 and 81.2581.25 on MATH500, so every run exceeds published power sampling (Appendix B.2). At temperature 11, this model gains 23.023.0 and 27.327.3 points over the untrained model and 11.011.0 and 11.611.6 points over ordinary on-policy distillation. Best-of-4 also rises on both benchmarks, so the model solves more problems rather than repeating the same answer. Lowering the temperature to 1/α1/\alpha requires no training, so comparing models at that temperature separates the contribution of training from that of decoding. At this temperature, ordinary on-policy distillation loses 1.91.9 and 1.81.8 points relative to the untrained model, both within one standard error, while oppd gains 8.48.4 and 15.015.0. The single-answer result also matches published GRPO on MATH500, 78.578.5 against 78.078.0 (Table 1). The published numbers come from a different evaluation protocol. Under ours, on the same 250250 problems, the sixteen-candidate sampler scores 79.279.2 and oppd 78.478.4 (Table 9). On 250250 MATH500 problems, sixteen candidates add 12.412.4 points for the untrained model, of which oppd obtains 11.611.6 (94%94\%) with a single generation. Running the sampler on the trained model adds only 1.61.6 more (Appendix B.1).

5.2 Comparison with training on verified rewards

GRPO shows how large a gain is usually available when reference answers can be used. We train the two methods from the same checkpoint to put oppd on that scale, not to argue that one should replace the other, and they compose.

We train oppd and GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) from the same Qwen3-8B-Base checkpoint for 300300 optimizer steps each. At each step, both draw two prompts and sample sixteen answers of at most 10241024 tokens per prompt, so each generates 9,6009{,}600 answers. Our GRPO is the standard version, with one optimization pass over each batch of samples and a binary reward from the evaluation grader. Both runs are small next to published GRPO training, 600600 prompt draws of at most 10241024 tokens each, so the comparison bounds neither method at a larger budget. oppd scores higher on all three benchmarks (Table 13), by 3.753.75 points on MATH500, 4.004.00 on GSM8K and 5.425.42 on AIME, each between one and two standard errors and all three with the same sign. GRPO learns only from groups of answers whose rewards differ, and 234234 of the 600600 groups (39%39\%) gave every answer the same reward and no gradient, while every prompt drawn produced a gradient for oppd (Appendix B.10).

The two methods also combine. Applied to a Qwen2.5-Math-7B checkpoint that GRPO had already trained from 50.2550.25 to 64.0064.00 on MATH500 and 59.2559.25 to 71.0071.00 on GSM8K, oppd adds 9.259.25 and 8.388.38 more, 3.13.1 and 2.82.8 standard errors (Table 7), and AIME pass@1 rises from 10.83%10.83\% with either method alone to 12.92%12.92\% with both (Appendix B.11).

5.3 Evidence that the student moves toward the power distribution

Training should reduce Dβ(πα∥pϕ)D_{\beta}(\pi_{\alpha}\|p_{\phi}), and (4) lets us check this on held-out problems by measuring ESS/N\mathrm{ESS}/N with each model as the proposal. The implied divergence D^2=−log⁡(ESS/N)\hat{D}_{2}=-\log(\mathrm{ESS}/N) falls by 21.6%21.6\% on Qwen2.5-Math-7B and by 26.6%26.6\%, 24.7%24.7\% and 12.6%12.6\% at N=4N=4, 1616 and 6464 on Qwen3-8B-Base. Along the answers of the model trained at λ=0\lambda=0, the untrained model’s token entropy is 0.320.32 times its entropy along its own answers, against 0.470.47 for ordinary on-policy distillation (Appendix B.3).

On the λ\lambda sweep, where Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B is trained with Qwen2.5-Math-7B as the teacher, the absorbed exponent decreases as λ\lambda increases across all five settings. It is 2.022.02 with the sequence-level term alone and 1.141.14 for ordinary on-policy distillation, and moving λ\lambda from 0.50.5 to 22 changes it only from 1.281.28 to 1.191.19 (Figure 2, Table 10). On contexts written by the initialization rather than by the model itself, ordinary distillation gives almost the same value and oppd does not (1.2071.207 against 2.0192.019), as expected when the signal comes only from the student’s own answers (Appendix B.4).

The best value of λ\lambda depends on the model, and the MATH500 gain an untrained model gets from lowering its temperature to 1/α1/\alpha predicts it. This gain is 19.919.9 points on Qwen2.5-Math-7B, which does best at λ=0\lambda=0, and 0.60.6 on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, which does best at λ=1\lambda=1 and loses 4.754.75 points of MATH500 without the anchor. A large gain means that sharpening is still available, so Qwen3-8B-Base (13.013.0) is trained at λ=0\lambda=0 (Appendix B.8).

5.4 Other models and scale

On Qwen3-8B-Base at temperature 11, oppd raises MATH500 from 65.5065.50 to 78.2578.25 and GSM8K from 78.0078.00 to 95.1395.13, which are 4.34.3 and 5.85.8 standard errors. Both scores are above ordinary on-policy distillation (75.0075.00 and 93.0093.00), and best-of-4 rises on both. On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct at λ=1\lambda=1, oppd gains 3.253.25 and 3.133.13 points over the untrained model and 2.752.75 on MATH500 over ordinary on-policy distillation (Table 11). On Qwen3-14B-Base at λ=0\lambda=0 and temperature 11, oppd reaches 84.0084.00 on MATH500, 95.8895.88 on GSM8K and 16.2516.25 on AIME, above the untrained model’s best at either temperature (82.0082.00, 92.3892.38 and 12.9212.92), and adds 18.5018.50 points on MATH500 against 12.7512.75 on Qwen3-8B-Base (Table 5).

deepseek-math-7b-rl (Shao et al., 2024), from a third family, was already trained with verified rewards, and lowering its temperature to 1/α1/\alpha gains +0.00+0.00 points on MATH500. oppd at the prescribed λ=1\lambda=1 raises MATH500 from 47.1247.12 to 51.5051.50 (95%95\% interval [+0.88,+7.88][+0.88,+7.88]) and GSM8K from 85.3885.38 to 87.7587.75 (Appendix B.7).

Because the method uses no reference answers, its training questions can come from any source: training Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on 40004000 OpenR1-Math-220k problem statements gives 51.1351.13 on MATH500 and 85.8885.88 on GSM8K, against 52.5052.50 and 85.3885.38 with GSM8K prompts (Appendix B.12).

5.5 Code generation

HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) scores a model’s implementation of a Python function, given its signature, by running unit tests. We evaluate the oppd checkpoints of four models (two for Qwen2.5-Math-7B) and the GRPO checkpoint of Section 5.2, each with its default generation configuration.

oppd raises HumanEval pass@1 on all four models, by 3.513.51 to 5.345.34 points (Table 2). The 95%95\% interval excludes zero in every case except Qwen2.5-Math-7B at λ=0\lambda=0, the setting of Table 1. The GRPO checkpoint gains 1.981.98 points, with an interval that includes zero.

6 Related work

Power sampling and sequential Monte Carlo.

Karan & Du (2026) introduce Metropolis–Hastings sampling from the power distribution (1) and show that it matches reinforcement-learning post-training on reasoning benchmarks. Azizi et al. (2026) replace the serial Markov chain with the batch-parallel sampler we use, and Ji et al. (2026) approximate the next-token distribution of πα\pi_{\alpha} with sampled continuations. All three methods run at inference time. Tomihari & Sato (2026) show that the power distribution is the closed-form optimum of KL-regularized reinforcement learning when the reward is the model’s own sequence log-probability, and derive power self-distillation, which trains a model on samples a power sampler produced and reaches accuracy at or above power sampling at much lower inference cost. Moving the cost of power sampling into training is therefore established. oppd differs in where the training answers come from and in what is optimized: the student is the sampler’s proposal distribution, so the answers are its own and one teacher pass per block serves both the sampler and the update, and the objective is the Rényi family (3) rather than supervised learning on stored samples. oppd trains on-policy, the setting for which on-policy distillation was introduced (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024). SMC has also been used to steer language models toward constraints (Lew et al., 2023) and for inference with learned twist functions (Zhao et al., 2024), and Hu et al. (2024) learn to sample intractable posteriors with GFlowNet objectives. We do not learn a twist function (Section 2.2).

Distillation and post-training.

Sequence-level knowledge distillation trains a student on answers generated by the teacher (Kim & Rush, 2016; Hinton et al., 2015), and on-policy variants train on answers the student generates and the teacher scores. Methods that use verified rewards, such as GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), need to know whether each answer is correct. Methods that reward a model’s own confidence instead include entropy minimization (Agarwal et al., 2025), self-certainty (Zhao et al., 2025), negative token entropy (Prabhudesai et al., 2025) and majority-vote rewards (Zuo et al., 2025), and Huang et al. (2025) analyze self-improvement as sharpening against the model’s own judgments. With the proposal of Theorem 1 and β=1\beta=1, (5) makes our training weight a softmax over the negative Rényi entropy accumulated along each answer, a confidence weighting whose scores come from a frozen teacher and are used inside a sampler. oppd needs only the questions, so it applies where those methods cannot be run, and it can also be applied to a model those methods have already trained. Yue et al. (2025) argue that such methods mostly re-weight answers the model could already produce, as power sampling does.

7 Conclusion

oppd trains a model toward the sequence-level power distribution of a teacher, so that one generation replaces the sampler. The trained model scores above published power sampling with 6464 candidates, matches GRPO trained from the same checkpoint and budget without reading reference answers, and improves a model that verified rewards have already trained. One loss coefficient controls the sharpening.

Appendix A The two-token example

Section 2.1 states that sharpening complete answers differs from sharpening tokens. The following example shows the difference on a small case.

Consider a vocabulary of two tokens and answers of length two, with p⁡(a)=0.6p(a)=0.6, p⁡(a∣a)=0.9p(a\mid a)=0.9 and p⁡(a∣b)=p⁡(b∣b)=0.5p(a\mid b)=p(b\mid b)=0.5. Multiplying gives p⁡(a​a)=0.54p(aa)=0.54, p⁡(a​b)=0.06p(ab)=0.06 and p⁡(b​a)=p⁡(b​b)=0.20p(ba)=p(bb)=0.20. Setting α=2\alpha=2:

a​aaa a​bab b​aba b​bbb total on answers starting with bb
power distribution, α=2\alpha=2 0.7770.777 0.0100.010 0.1070.107 0.1070.107 0.2130.213
temperature τ=1/2\tau=1/2 0.6840.684 0.0080.008 0.1540.154 0.1540.154 0.3080.308

The power distribution assigns less probability to answers beginning with bb, 0.2130.213 against 0.3080.308. It does so because every continuation of bb is uncertain, so no answer beginning with bb can reach a high total probability. Temperature cannot represent this, because at the first token it compares 0.60.6 against 0.40.4 with no information about the answers those two tokens lead to. The power distribution accounts for how probable the continuations of each prefix are, and temperature does not. This is the information that oppd transfers into the model parameters.

Appendix B Extended experimental results

This appendix gives in full the results summarized in Section 5.

B.1 Running the sampler on the trained model

On the untrained model, sixteen candidates add 12.412.4 points. With a single generation, oppd obtains 11.611.6 of these 12.412.4 points (94%94\%), and running the sampler on the trained model adds only 1.61.6 more (Figure 3). Figure 1c shows the same comparison, between a sampler run on every query before training and one ordinary generation after it. The gain from candidates falls from 12.412.4 to 5.25.2 to 1.61.6 points as training places more weight on the sequence-level term (untrained, λ=1\lambda=1, λ=0\lambda=0). The N=1N{=}1 value of 78.478.4 here and the 78.5078.50 of Table 1 are both the MATH500 accuracy of the same trained model generating one answer at temperature 1/α1/\alpha, measured under two protocols: 250250 problems with one sample, and 200200 problems with four. The two values agree to within 0.10.1 points, which checks the two protocols against each other.

B.2 Training seeds

We trained the configuration of Table 1 with two further random seeds under the settings of Section 5. Sampled at temperature 1/α1/\alpha, the three runs score 78.5078.50 to 81.2581.25 on MATH500 and 91.1391.13 to 92.6392.63 on GSM8K (Table 3). Every run exceeds published power sampling with 6464 candidates, by 2.42.4 to 5.25.2 points on MATH500 and 3.53.5 to 5.05.0 on GSM8K, and every run matches or exceeds published GRPO on MATH500. At temperature 11 the gain over the untrained model is 21.321.3 to 24.424.4 points on MATH500 and 26.626.6 to 30.330.3 on GSM8K.

B.3 Divergence and entropy measurements

Training should reduce Dβ(πα∥pϕ)D_{\beta}(\pi_{\alpha}\|p_{\phi}), and identity (4) lets us check this independently on held-out problems by reading the ESS when each model is the proposal distribution. We write D^2=−log⁡(ESS/N)\hat{D}_{2}=-\log(\mathrm{ESS}/N) for the divergence that this identity implies, which is (3) at β=2\beta=2 between πα\pi_{\alpha} and the model used as the proposal. The measured divergence falls by 21.6%21.6\%, and it falls more at λ=0\lambda=0 than at λ=1\lambda=1 (Table 4, left).

The first row of this table needs explanation. Its proposal distribution is the teacher at temperature 1/α1/\alpha, which Theorem 1 identifies as the best proposal among those that depend only on the prefix, and yet both trained models do better. This does not contradict the theorem, which fixes a prefix and minimizes the variance of the next incremental importance weight. The variation that remains, described by (5), comes from differences between the prefixes that different candidates reach. A trained model cannot improve on q⋆q^{\star} at a fixed prefix, but it can write answers whose prefixes give more uniform importance weights. The right half of Table 4 measures this effect. Sharpening complete answers favors answers of high total probability, which by (5) are answers along which the teacher is confident throughout. Along the answers written by the model trained at λ=0\lambda=0, the untrained model’s token entropy is 0.320.32 times its entropy along its own answers, against 0.470.47 for ordinary on-policy distillation. Of the three models, the most accurate has the lowest ratio.

B.4 The coefficient λ\lambda controls the absorbed exponent

The absorbed exponent decreases as λ\lambda increases, across all five settings (Figure 2a). With the sequence-level term alone it rises by 1.021.02 above one, to about half of α\alpha, against a rise of 0.140.14 for ordinary on-policy distillation. The interquartile ranges of the two extreme settings do not overlap. The relationship is not linear: removing the anchor entirely moves αeff\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}} from 1.281.28 to 2.022.02, whereas moving λ\lambda from 0.50.5 to 22 moves it only from 1.281.28 to 1.191.19. Even a small coefficient on the mass-covering anchor suppresses most of the available sharpening, which is consistent with its forward-KL form.

The change appears on the answers the student writes.

The estimator can be run on two sets of contexts. One set comes from answers written by the initialization, and the other from answers written by the trained model itself. The two estimates agree for ordinary on-policy distillation (1.1051.105 and 1.1441.144) and differ for oppd (1.2071.207 and 2.0192.019) (Table 10, right, and Figure 2b). Measuring on a model’s own answers therefore does not raise the estimate in general, only for the model trained with the sequence-level term. On-policy training predicts this asymmetry. The training signal comes only from answers that the student generates, so the parameters should change mainly along those answers, and a method trained on text written by the teacher would not produce this pattern.

B.5 Replication on two further models

On Qwen3-8B-Base, oppd gains 12.7512.75 and 17.1317.13 points over the untrained model, which are 4.34.3 and 5.85.8 standard errors, and best-of-4 rises on both benchmarks. The divergence measurement gives the same result for every number of candidates we tested: D^2\hat{D}_{2} falls from 0.4940.494 to 0.3620.362 at N=4N{=}4, from 0.7120.712 to 0.5360.536 at N=16N{=}16, and from 0.8510.851 to 0.7440.744 at N=64N{=}64. These are reductions of 26.6%26.6\%, 24.7%24.7\% and 12.6%12.6\%, consistent with the 21.6%21.6\% measured on Qwen2.5-Math-7B. Values of D^2\hat{D}_{2} are not comparable across numbers of candidates, because more candidates explore more of the distribution, so each comparison is made at a fixed NN.

On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, oppd gains 3.253.25 and 3.133.13 points over the untrained model, and 2.752.75 points on MATH500 over ordinary on-policy distillation. The two methods differ more in best-of-4 than in pass@1: ordinary on-policy distillation lowers MATH500 best-of-4 by 4.04.0 points relative to the untrained model, while oppd lowers it by 1.01.0.

B.6 Scaling to a larger model

The models above have 77 to 88B parameters. To test whether the method still works at a larger scale, we ran it on Qwen3-14B-Base, whose authors report it as comparable to Qwen2.5-32B-Base (Yang et al., 2025). All settings were those of Section 5 except the learning rate, which was 3×10−63\times 10^{-6}. We used λ=0\lambda=0, as the rule of Appendix B.8 prescribes, and evaluated both the untrained and the trained model at both decoding temperatures.

With both models sampled at temperature 1/α1/\alpha, oppd gains 3.503.50 points on MATH500, 3.373.37 on GSM8K and 2.502.50 on AIME (Table 5). The more informative comparison is across the two temperatures. Lowering the temperature requires no training and raises the untrained model to 82.0082.00, 92.3892.38 and 12.9212.92, its better result of the two temperatures we evaluate. oppd sampled at temperature 11, without any change to decoding, reaches 84.0084.00, 95.8895.88 and 16.2516.25, above the untrained model’s best on every benchmark.

oppd also keeps more of the model’s diversity, as measured by best-of-4, than lowering the temperature does. Lowering the temperature reduces the untrained model’s best-of-4 on two of the three benchmarks, from 97.597.5 to 96.096.0 on GSM8K and from 25.025.0 to 20.020.0 on AIME, a cost of the higher pass@1 that a lower temperature gives. oppd at temperature 11 scores 93.093.0, 97.097.0 and 28.328.3 in best-of-4, above the untrained model at either temperature on MATH500 and AIME. The gains are largest on MATH500, where oppd adds 18.5018.50 points at temperature 11, against the 12.7512.75 it adds on Qwen3-8B-Base.

B.7 A third model family

deepseek-math-7b-rl differs from the models above in two ways that matter for this measurement. It comes from a third model family, and it has already been trained with verified rewards on mathematics, so reinforcement learning has already moved its probability toward correct answers.

Before training, lowering its sampling temperature from 11 to 1/α1/\alpha leaves MATH500 at 47.1247.12 and moves GSM8K from 85.3885.38 to 86.0086.00, gains of +0.00+0.00 and +0.62+0.62 points. The rule of Appendix B.8 prescribes λ=1\lambda=1 for a model that gains this little from a lower temperature, and we fixed λ=1\lambda=1 from this measurement before training began.

oppd scores above the untrained model in every row of Table 6. At temperature 11, MATH500 rises 4.384.38 points with a 95%95\% interval of [+0.88,+7.88][+0.88,+7.88], and GSM8K rises 2.382.38 points.

This model allows a direct comparison of the two operations of Section 2.1. Lowering the temperature, the token-level operation, gives +0.00+0.00 points on MATH500. Sequence-level sharpening through oppd gives 4.384.38 points on the same benchmark and the same problems. On a model where token-level sharpening gives no further gain, sequence-level sharpening still raises accuracy.

B.8 Choosing λ\lambda from the untrained model

Removing the anchor term costs Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct 4.754.75 points of MATH500 accuracy and 5.55.5 points of best-of-4. On Qwen2.5-Math-7B the same change gains 9.259.25 points, so the best coefficient differs between models. A quantity measured on the untrained model predicts which case applies: how much the model gains from lowering its sampling temperature, which reflects how much sharpening is still available.

model MATH500 gain from temperature 1/α1/\alpha better λ\lambda
Qwen2.5-Math-7B +19.9+19.9 00
Qwen3-8B-Base +13.0+13.0 00 (only λ\lambda trained)
Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct +0.6+0.6 11

A model that gains a lot from a lower temperature still has sharpening available and tolerates λ=0\lambda=0, the strongest setting. A model that gains almost nothing is already sharp, and sharpening it further costs accuracy and best-of-4. On these three models, a single evaluation of the untrained model identifies the better λ\lambda.

B.9 Applying oppd after training with verified rewards

Table 1 compares our result with published GRPO on the same model. Reinforcement learning with verified rewards and oppd might move probability toward the same answers, in which case applying one after the other would give no further gain. We tested this by taking a checkpoint of Qwen2.5-Math-7B that had already been trained with GRPO on verified rewards and training it further with oppd. All other settings were those of Section 5.

Training with verified rewards moves the untrained model from 50.2550.25 to 64.0064.00 on MATH500 and from 59.2559.25 to 71.0071.00 on GSM8K. oppd then adds a further 9.259.25 and 8.388.38 points, which are 3.13.1 and 2.82.8 standard errors (Table 7). Both settings of λ\lambda give gains of a similar size, 8.128.12 and 8.758.75 points at λ=1\lambda=1, so this model is not sensitive to the anchor coefficient in the way that the instruction-tuned model of Appendix B.8 was.

The two procedures can therefore be combined: training with verified rewards does not already provide what oppd adds, although both start from the same untrained model and improve the same benchmarks. Because the two gains add up, oppd is useful both where verified rewards are unavailable, as in Table 1, and as a further step after training with them.

B.10 Equal-budget comparison with GRPO

Appendix B.9 applied oppd to a checkpoint that others had trained with GRPO. This shows that the two can be combined, but it does not say how large the gain from oppd is beside a method that reads reference answers. Here we train both ourselves, from the same starting model and with the same budget. The comparison uses one standard implementation of GRPO at one budget, and we draw no conclusion from it about the wider family of reinforcement-learning methods that use verified rewards.

What is held equal.

Both methods run for 300300 optimizer steps. At each step both draw two prompts and sample sixteen answers of at most 10241024 tokens per prompt, so each method generates 9,6009{,}600 answers over the run. GRPO additionally uses a reference answer for every training question, which oppd never does.

Our GRPO implementation is the standard one, with a single optimization pass over each batch of samples. For each prompt it samples sixteen answers, called a group, and scores each with a binary reward from the grader used for evaluation. The advantage of each answer is its reward minus the group mean, divided by the group standard deviation. With a single pass, the model that generated the samples is the model being updated, so the ratio between the new and the sampling probabilities is one and the clipping range is inactive.

oppd scores higher on all three benchmarks (Figure 6), by 3.753.75 points on MATH500, 4.004.00 on GSM8K and 5.425.42 on AIME. Each margin is between one and two standard errors, so none is conclusive on its own, but all three favor the method that uses no reference answers.

Best-of-4, shown as the pale extensions in Figure 6, separates the two methods more clearly than pass@1. On MATH500 and GSM8K both methods raise it, GRPO by 0.50.5 and 1.01.0 points and oppd by 1.51.5 and 2.52.5. On AIME they differ: GRPO leaves best-of-4 at 16.6716.67, the same as the untrained model, while oppd raises it to 26.6726.67. A method that raises pass@1 without raising best-of-4 selects more reliably among answers the model could already produce. Raising both means that the model solves problems it did not solve in four attempts before, and on the hardest of the three benchmarks only oppd does so. AIME has only 6060 problems, so the pass@1 margins there are imprecise.

Groups that give GRPO no training signal.

GRPO learns from a group only when the rewards in it differ. If all sixteen answers earn the same reward, the group mean equals every reward, all advantages are zero, and the prompt contributes no gradient. Our logs record how often this happened: 234234 of GRPO’s 600600 prompt draws (39%39\%) had uniform rewards and produced no gradient. These draws still cost computation, because the answers had to be generated before their rewards could be compared.

This fraction is higher than the average reward rate would suggest. Late in training, the mean reward ranged from 0.060.06 to 0.970.97 across steps. If every answer succeeded independently at the average of these rates, fewer than 2%2\% of groups of sixteen would have uniform rewards. Observing 39%39\% therefore means that difficulty is not spread evenly across prompts. A given problem tends to be either easy for the model, so that most of the sixteen answers succeed, or too hard, so that almost none do. Both cases tend to give uniform rewards and zero advantages, so mainly problems of intermediate difficulty provide a learning signal.

oppd does not have this problem, because its training weights come from the teacher’s probabilities rather than from a correctness check. Sixteen answers that are all incorrect still differ in the total probability the teacher assigns them, so their training weights still differ. The measured ESS stayed between 0.39​N0.39N and 0.64​N0.64N throughout training, so no group’s weight concentrated on a single candidate, and every prompt drawn produced a gradient.

The two methods also place different requirements on the training data. GRPO needs a reference answer that a grader can check, and of the 12,00012{,}000 OpenR1-Math-220k items we examined, 8,2368{,}236 had one. The rest give their answer in a form that the grader cannot match to a single expression, such as a pair of values or a multiple-choice letter. oppd uses only the question, so all 12,00012{,}000 items were available to it.

B.11 Results on AIME

MATH500 and GSM8K are solved often enough by the untrained model that a large part of each score is already available before training. We therefore also evaluate on AIME, a competition benchmark on which a 77B model rarely succeeds. We pool the 20242024 and 20252025 problem sets, giving 6060 problems, and generate four answers for each. All rows use the same 35003500-token generation limit, which keeps the prompt and the answer inside the model’s context window.

The untrained model solves 4.17%4.17\% of AIME problems on a single attempt. Training it with GRPO on verified rewards raises that to 10.83%10.83\%, and oppd, which uses no reference answers, reaches the same 10.83%10.83\% (Figure 5). The two methods reach this number with different requirements: GRPO needs to know whether every training answer was correct, while oppd needs only the questions.

Applying oppd after GRPO exceeds either method alone, reaching 12.92%12.92\%. Best-of-4 separates the three more clearly, at 21.6721.67 for GRPO, 20.0020.00 for oppd, and 31.6731.67 for the two together. The combined model solves 31.67%31.67\% of these problems within four attempts, where the untrained model solves 13.33%13.33\%, so it solves problems that the untrained model does not solve in four attempts. Selecting among answers the untrained model already produces cannot give such a gain.

The AIME result holds on a second model.

We repeated the evaluation on Qwen3-8B-Base, a stronger and more recent starting point than Qwen2.5-Math-7B. The untrained model solves 7.08%7.08\% of AIME problems on a single attempt, and oppd raises that to 14.17%14.17\%, with best-of-4 going from 16.6716.67 to 26.6726.67. Single-answer accuracy at least doubles on both models, and 14.17%14.17\% is the highest AIME result among our 77B and 88B models, so the pattern does not depend on starting from a model that rarely solves these problems.

The gain also transfers to problems harder than those used in training. The training prompts are GSM8K questions, which are grade-school word problems, while the gain appears on competition problems that the model solves only occasionally.

B.12 Training on a different prompt source

Because the method uses no reference answers, the training questions can come from any source. We repeated the training on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using 40004000 problem statements from OpenR1-Math-220k (Hugging Face, 2025). A corpus assembled from competition sources may contain problems that also appear in the benchmark. We therefore removed every training prompt whose normalized form matched an evaluation problem, so no benchmark question appeared during training.

Training on this corpus gives results within one standard error of training on GSM8K questions: MATH500 is 51.1351.13 against 52.5052.50 and GSM8K is 85.8885.88 against 85.3885.38, differences of 1.41.4 and 0.50.5 points against a standard error of 2.92.9. Of the configurations trained on this model, this one also has the highest best-of-4 (tied on GSM8K): 69.069.0 against the untrained model’s 69.569.5 on MATH500, and 94.094.0 against 92.592.5 on GSM8K, while pass@1 rises on both benchmarks. One training run per model, on questions from any source, is therefore sufficient. The method needs a supply of questions, not questions matched to the evaluation.

B.13 Training against the student itself or a larger teacher

Our main results use the student as its own teacher. Section 5 chose self-distillation for a measurement reason: αeff​(pbase→pT)\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(p_{\mathrm{base}}\to p_{\mathrm{T}}) is then exactly 1.0001.000, so no measured sharpening can come from copying a stronger model. The choice also follows from the purpose of the method: oppd redistributes probability that the student already assigns, so the distribution that should be sharpened is the student’s own.

Standard distillation practice suggests the opposite, namely that a larger teacher should do better. We tested this on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, training it twice for 300300 steps with λ=1\lambda=1 and otherwise identical settings, once against Qwen2.5-Math-7B as teacher and once against itself.

Both settings improve on the untrained model, by 8.508.50 and 9.759.75 points with the larger teacher and by 10.1310.13 and 15.3715.37 points with the student itself (Table 8). Self-distillation is ahead by 5.625.62 points on GSM8K, which is 1.51.5 standard errors, and by 1.631.63 on MATH500, which is within noise. The two benchmarks together show that scoring against the student’s own distribution loses nothing relative to a teacher four times its size, and on one benchmark it does better.

This agrees with how the method works. oppd uses the scoring model’s ranking of complete answers, and that ranking indicates where to move probability only if the probability belongs to the model being trained. A larger teacher defines a power distribution that is not the student’s own, so part of the gradient goes into closing the gap between the two models rather than into sharpening the student. Self-distillation removes this competing objective, so the method does not need a larger model to learn from.

Both runs used λ=1\lambda=1, chosen for the larger-teacher setting. We did not test whether λ=0\lambda=0 changes their order, or how the comparison changes as the gap between teacher and student grows.

B.14 Where the sampler’s gain comes from

Grading every candidate separates two things that the sampler does: it discards candidates while answers are being written, and at the end it re-ranks the finished answers by importance weight. If the importance weights carried information about correctness, the total normalized weight on correct candidates would exceed the fraction of candidates that are correct. Across eleven measurements spanning three models and three numbers of candidates, the two agree to within 0.50.5 points in every case. This includes self-distillation, where teacher and student share an architecture. Choosing the answer by weighted draw, by highest weight, or by majority vote gives the same result throughout (Appendix R).

The teacher’s probabilities therefore carry no useful information for ranking finished answers. All of the sampler’s gain comes from discarding candidates while the answers are still being written and their continuations still differ. Once the answers are complete, the teacher’s probabilities no longer separate correct from incorrect candidates. This has a consequence for a family of methods: re-ranking complete answers by model probability should not be expected to help, whereas intervening during generation should.

Appendix E Notation and definitions

This section defines the terms used in the paper, for readers who are not familiar with all of them.

Prompts, answers, probabilities.

xx is the prompt, y=(y1,…,yT)y=(y_{1},\dots,y_{T}) an answer of TT tokens, and y<ty_{<t} the prefix before position tt. A token is a short piece of text. A language model factors p⁡(y∣x)=∏tp⁡(yt∣x,y<t)p(y\mid x)=\prod_{t}p(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t}), and p(⋅∣x,y<t)p(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t}), as a function of the next token, is a next-token distribution.

Temperature.

Sampling at temperature τ\tau replaces each next-token distribution p⁡(⋅)p(\cdot) by one proportional to p​(⋅)1/τp(\cdot)^{1/\tau}. Temperature τ=1\tau=1 is ordinary sampling, and τ<1\tau<1 makes likely tokens more likely, which is token-level sharpening. The power distribution sharpens complete answers instead (Section 2.1).

pass@1 and best-of-4.

We draw four independent answers per problem. pass@1 is the fraction correct, averaged over problems; it estimates the chance a single answer is correct. best-of-4 counts a problem solved if at least one of the four is correct. A method that raises pass@1 while best-of-4 holds or rises is solving more problems. A method that raises pass@1 while best-of-4 falls is producing the same answer more consistently. The gap between the two metrics shows how much the model’s success depends on which sample is drawn.

Entropy and nats.

Entropy measures how spread out a distribution is, and it is zero when one outcome is certain. We report it in nats, the unit that natural logarithms give. For the models studied here, a next-token entropy of a few tenths of a nat means that the model is already confident.

Divergences.

KL(P∥Q)\mathrm{KL}(P\|Q) measures how different PP is from QQ. It is zero if and only if the two agree, and it is not symmetric, so the two orderings behave differently as objectives. Forward KL, KL(P∥Q)\mathrm{KL}(P\|Q) with PP the distribution being approximated, is mass-covering: it heavily penalizes QQ for assigning little probability where PP assigns some, and it tolerates QQ being broad. Reverse KL, KL(Q∥P)\mathrm{KL}(Q\|P), is mode-seeking: it penalizes QQ for assigning probability where PP assigns little. The Rényi divergence Dβ(P∥Q)=1β−1log∑yP(y)βQ(y)1−βD_{\beta}(P\|Q)=\tfrac{1}{\beta-1}\log\sum_{y}P(y)^{\beta}Q(y)^{1-\beta} is a family indexed by β>0\beta>0, equal to KL at β=1\beta=1; it is zero exactly when P=QP=Q and positive otherwise. The Rényi entropy is Hα​(p)=11−α​log​∑vp​(v)αH_{\alpha}(p)=\tfrac{1}{1-\alpha}\log\sum_{v}p(v)^{\alpha}.

Distillation.

Distillation trains a student pϕp_{\phi}, with parameters ϕ\phi, to behave like a teacher pTp_{\mathrm{T}}. In off-policy distillation the teacher writes examples and the student reproduces them. In on-policy distillation the student writes answers and the teacher scores them, so the student learns to continue from its own mistakes. Self-distillation initializes both from the same model, which rules out that a measured change comes from the student copying a stronger model.

Stop-gradient.

[⋅]sg[\cdot]_{\mathrm{sg}} denotes a quantity held fixed during differentiation.

Uncertainty.

With 200200 problems and four samples each, the paired standard error on a difference between two methods on the same problems is ≈2.9\approx 2.9 points, written 1​σ1\sigma. Differences of 1​σ1\sigma or less are not treated as real. For per-context estimates we report the interquartile range (IQR), the range of the middle half of the measurements.

Appendix F Extended background on the sampler

Importance sampling.

To estimate averages under a distribution π=γ/Z\pi=\gamma/Z, where γ\gamma can be evaluated but ZZ cannot, draw samples from a proposal distribution qq and weight each sample by w⁡(y)=γ⁡(y)/q⁡(y)w(y)=\gamma(y)/q(y), which measures how much more π\pi favors the sample than qq does. The self-normalized estimate is 𝔼π​[f]≈∑iw⁡(y(i))​f​(y(i))/∑iw⁡(y(i))\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[f]\approx\sum_{i}w(y^{(i)})f(y^{(i)})/\sum_{i}w(y^{(i)}), and the division removes ZZ. This estimator is consistent rather than unbiased, with bias of order 1/N1/N.

Computing the weights incrementally.

When importance sampling is applied to complete answers in one step, the weights vary over many orders of magnitude and one sample dominates. Defining unnormalized distributions over prefixes, γt(y1:t)=pT(y1:t∣x)α\gamma_{t}(y_{1:t})=p_{\mathrm{T}}(y_{1:t}\mid x)^{\alpha}, and updating the weights by (2) gives the same total weight γT/q\gamma_{T}/q, while letting the sampler monitor the weights and resample during generation.

Resampling.

When the ESS falls below κ​N\kappa N (we use κ=0.5\kappa=0.5), the candidates are resampled with probability proportional to their normalized importance weights, and all weights are reset to be equal. We use systematic resampling, which is unbiased and has lower variance than multinomial resampling (Doucet & Johansen, 2009). Duplicated candidates diverge again because their next tokens are sampled independently. Any unbiased resampling scheme leaves the distribution being approximated unchanged and affects only the variance and the diversity of the candidates.

What the weights select for.

Equation (5) states that, under the variance-optimal proposal, a candidate’s log importance weight is (1−α)(1-\alpha) times the sum of the Rényi entropies of the teacher’s next-token distributions along its answer. Since α>1\alpha>1 makes (1−α)(1-\alpha) negative, candidates whose prefixes the teacher is confident about keep their weight, and candidates that pass through uncertain positions lose it. No reward model, verifier or reference answer is used at any point.

Appendix G Why a weighted token-level KL cannot reach the power distribution

An alternative objective multiplies a per-token KL divergence to the teacher at temperature 1/α1/\alpha by the training weight of each answer, ∑i,t[A¯(i)]sgKL(πT(α)(⋅∣y<t(i))∥pϕ(⋅∣y<t(i)))\sum_{i,t}[\bar{A}^{(i)}]_{\mathrm{sg}}\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi^{(\alpha)}_{\mathrm{T}}(\cdot\mid y^{(i)}_{<t})\|p_{\phi}(\cdot\mid y^{(i)}_{<t})). This objective cannot reach πα\pi_{\alpha}. A divergence multiplied by a nonnegative scalar has the same minimizer as the divergence itself, so for every context cc that is visited, the optimal pϕ(⋅∣c)p_{\phi}(\cdot\mid c) is πT(α)(⋅∣c)\pi^{(\alpha)}_{\mathrm{T}}(\cdot\mid c) whatever the weights are. Weights placed outside a divergence change which contexts contribute, but they never change the distribution matched at each context. The attainable optimum is therefore the teacher at temperature 1/α1/\alpha, which Section 2.1 shows differs from πα\pi_{\alpha}.

The underlying reason is that the next-token distribution of πα\pi_{\alpha} is proportional to pT(v∣y<t)αVt(y1:tv)p_{\mathrm{T}}(v\mid y_{<t})^{\alpha}\,V_{t}(y_{1:t}v), where the twist function Vt=∑y>tpT(y>t∣y1:t)αV_{t}=\sum_{y_{>t}}p_{\mathrm{T}}(y_{>t}\mid y_{1:t})^{\alpha} sums over all continuations. Setting Vt≡constV_{t}\equiv\mathrm{const} leaves exactly the teacher at temperature 1/α1/\alpha, and a factor missing inside the divergence cannot be supplied by a weight outside it. Equation (9) instead places the weights on a log-likelihood, where they change the distribution being fitted.

This appendix derives the loss from the objective step by step. It repeats material from Section 3 in a form that can be checked line by line, and it contains no new results.

where the dependence on xx is omitted. Minimizing 𝒥\mathcal{J} is equivalent to minimizing log⁡S\log S when β>1\beta>1 and to maximizing it when β<1\beta<1; the factor 1β−1\tfrac{1}{\beta-1} handles the sign, which is why the gradient below has one form for every β\beta.

∇ϕS=(1−β)​∑yπα​(y)β​pϕ​(y)1−β​∇ϕ​log⁡pϕ​(y).\nabla_{\phi}S\;=\;(1-\beta)\sum_{y}\pi_{\alpha}(y)^{\beta}\,p_{\phi}(y)^{1-\beta}\,\nabla_{\phi}\log p_{\phi}(y).

Now differentiate 𝒥=1β−1​log⁡S\mathcal{J}=\tfrac{1}{\beta-1}\log S:

∇ϕ𝒥=1β−1⋅∇ϕSS=1−ββ−1​∑yπα​(y)β​pϕ​(y)1−βS​∇ϕ​log⁡pϕ​(y).\nabla_{\phi}\mathcal{J}\;=\;\frac{1}{\beta-1}\cdot\frac{\nabla_{\phi}S}{S}\;=\;\frac{1-\beta}{\beta-1}\sum_{y}\frac{\pi_{\alpha}(y)^{\beta}\,p_{\phi}(y)^{1-\beta}}{S}\,\nabla_{\phi}\log p_{\phi}(y).

The prefactor 1−ββ−1\tfrac{1-\beta}{\beta-1} equals −1-1 for every β≠1\beta\neq 1. Define

π¯(β)​(y)=πα​(y)β​pϕ​(y)1−βS,\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)}(y)\;=\;\frac{\pi_{\alpha}(y)^{\beta}\,p_{\phi}(y)^{1-\beta}}{S},

which is nonnegative and sums to one over yy, so it is a probability distribution. Then

∇ϕDβ(πα∥pϕ)=−∑yπ¯(β)(y)∇ϕlogpϕ(y)=−𝔼π¯(β)[∇ϕlogpϕ(y)],\nabla_{\phi}D_{\beta}(\pi_{\alpha}\|p_{\phi})\;=\;-\sum_{y}\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)}(y)\,\nabla_{\phi}\log p_{\phi}(y)\;=\;-\,\mathbb{E}_{\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)}}\!\left[\nabla_{\phi}\log p_{\phi}(y)\right], (11)

which is Theorem 2. The case β=1\beta=1 follows by continuity and gives the gradient of KL(πα∥pϕ)\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{\alpha}\|p_{\phi}).

Substituting πα=pTα/Zα\pi_{\alpha}=p_{\mathrm{T}}^{\alpha}/Z_{\alpha} into the definition of π¯(β)\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)} gives π¯(β)∝pTα​β​pϕ1−β\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)}\propto p_{\mathrm{T}}^{\alpha\beta}\,p_{\phi}^{1-\beta}, with the factor Zα−βZ_{\alpha}^{-\beta} absorbed into the normalizer SS. This is why the intractable ZαZ_{\alpha} never appears in the gradient even though it appears in the objective.

H.3 Why the weights can be treated as constants

Equation (11) contains π¯(β)\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)}, which depends on ϕ\phi through pϕ1−βp_{\phi}^{1-\beta}. It might appear that differentiating a loss whose weights are computed from ϕ\phi and then held fixed would miss a term. It does not, because (11) is already the complete gradient. The differentiation in Appendix H.2 was applied to the full expression for 𝒥\mathcal{J}, including the dependence of π¯(β)\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)} on ϕ\phi, and every resulting term was collected. In the right-hand side, π¯(β)\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)} appears only as a weight. Any implementation that evaluates those weights and holds them fixed while differentiating log⁡pϕ\log p_{\phi} therefore computes (11) exactly, not an approximation of it. Appendix O confirms this numerically against brute-force enumeration.

H.4 From an expectation to a weighted average

We cannot evaluate the sum in (11), because it runs over every possible answer, and we cannot draw samples from π¯(β)\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)}, because computing its normalizer SS requires the same sum. Instead, we draw answers from a proposal distribution qq and correct for the mismatch.

Let y(1),…,y(N)y^{(1)},\dots,y^{(N)} be answers drawn from qq, and suppose q⁡(y)>0q(y)>0 wherever π¯(β)​(y)>0\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)}(y)>0. For any function ff,

𝔼π¯(β)​[f⁡(y)]=∑yπ¯(β)​(y)​f​(y)=∑yq⁡(y)​π¯(β)​(y)q⁡(y)​f​(y)=𝔼q​[π¯(β)​(y)q⁡(y)​f​(y)],\mathbb{E}_{\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)}}[f(y)]\;=\;\sum_{y}\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)}(y)\,f(y)\;=\;\sum_{y}q(y)\,\frac{\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)}(y)}{q(y)}\,f(y)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{q}\!\left[\frac{\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)}(y)}{q(y)}\,f(y)\right],

where the middle step multiplies and divides by q⁡(y)q(y), which is legitimate because q⁡(y)>0q(y)>0 on the support. The ratio π¯(β)​(y)/q​(y)\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)}(y)/q(y) is the importance weight of yy for estimating expectations under π¯(β)\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)}. We call its self-normalized version the training weight, to keep it distinct from the sampler’s importance weight for πα\pi_{\alpha}.

Two problems remain: the right-hand side is still an expectation, which we replace by the sample average over the NN answers, and π¯(β)\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)} is known only up to the constant SS, which we cannot compute. The self-normalized form handles both. Write A~(i)=π¯(β)​(y(i))/q⁡(y(i))\tilde{A}^{(i)}=\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)}(y^{(i)})/q(y^{(i)}) for the unnormalized ratio, using any convenient constant multiple of π¯(β)\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)}, and let

A¯(i)=A~(i)∑j=1NA~(j),so that∑i=1NA¯(i)=1.\bar{A}^{(i)}\;=\;\frac{\tilde{A}^{(i)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\tilde{A}^{(j)}},\qquad\text{so that}\qquad\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bar{A}^{(i)}=1.

Any constant common to all A~(i)\tilde{A}^{(i)} cancels between the numerator and the denominator, so the unknown SS and the unknown Zα−βZ_{\alpha}^{-\beta} both drop out. The self-normalized estimate is

𝔼π¯(β)​[f⁡(y)]≈∑i=1NA¯(i)​f​(y(i)),\mathbb{E}_{\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)}}[f(y)]\;\approx\;\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bar{A}^{(i)}f\big(y^{(i)}\big),

which is consistent, with bias of order 1/N1/N (Doucet et al., 2001). This is the sense in which Section 3.4 obtains the training weights from self-normalized importance sampling: they are the ratios π¯(β)/q\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)}/q evaluated at the sampled answers and rescaled to sum to one. Taking f=∇ϕ​log​pϕf=\nabla_{\phi}\log p_{\phi} and substituting into (11),

∇ϕDβ(πα∥pϕ)≈−∑i=1NA¯(i)∇ϕlogpϕ(y(i)).\nabla_{\phi}D_{\beta}(\pi_{\alpha}\|p_{\phi})\;\approx\;-\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bar{A}^{(i)}\,\nabla_{\phi}\log p_{\phi}\big(y^{(i)}\big). (12)

H.5 Computing the weights token by token

Both π¯(β)\bar{\pi}^{(\beta)} and qq factor over tokens, so their ratio does too. Writing the factorization out,

A~(i)∝∏tpT​(yt(i)∣x,y<t(i))α​β​∏tpϕ​(yt(i)∣x,y<t(i))1−β∏tqt​(yt(i)∣x,y<t(i)),\tilde{A}^{(i)}\;\propto\;\frac{\prod_{t}p_{\mathrm{T}}\big(y^{(i)}_{t}\mid x,y^{(i)}_{<t}\big)^{\alpha\beta}\prod_{t}p_{\phi}\big(y^{(i)}_{t}\mid x,y^{(i)}_{<t}\big)^{1-\beta}}{\prod_{t}q_{t}\big(y^{(i)}_{t}\mid x,y^{(i)}_{<t}\big)},

and taking logarithms turns each product into a sum:

logA~(i)=∑t[αβlogpT(yt(i)∣⋅)+(1−β)logpϕ(yt(i)∣⋅)−logqt(yt(i)∣⋅)],\log\tilde{A}^{(i)}=\sum_{t}\Big[\alpha\beta\log p_{\mathrm{T}}\big(y^{(i)}_{t}\mid\cdot\big)+(1-\beta)\log p_{\phi}\big(y^{(i)}_{t}\mid\cdot\big)-\log q_{t}\big(y^{(i)}_{t}\mid\cdot\big)\Big],

which is (8). Working in logarithms is necessary, because each factor is a probability below one and the product underflows to zero in floating point after a few hundred tokens. The three quantities in the bracket are the same three that the sampler evaluates at every token, which is the sense in which the sampler and the loss share their computation.

H.6 From the gradient to a scalar loss

Equation (12) is a gradient estimate, but automatic differentiation requires a scalar loss. Consider

ℒseq(ϕ)=−∑i=1N[A¯(i)]sglogpϕ(y(i)∣x),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{seq}}(\phi)\;=\;-\sum_{i=1}^{N}\big[\bar{A}^{(i)}\big]_{\mathrm{sg}}\,\log p_{\phi}\big(y^{(i)}\mid x\big),

where [⋅]sg[\cdot]_{\mathrm{sg}} means the enclosed value is treated as a constant by the differentiation. Differentiating, the constants pass through and

∇ϕℒseq=−∑i=1NA¯(i)∇ϕlogpϕ(y(i)∣x),\nabla_{\phi}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{seq}}\;=\;-\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bar{A}^{(i)}\,\nabla_{\phi}\log p_{\phi}\big(y^{(i)}\mid x\big),

which is exactly the right-hand side of (12). A gradient step on ℒseq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{seq}} is therefore a gradient step on Dβ(πα∥pϕ)D_{\beta}(\pi_{\alpha}\|p_{\phi}), up to the error of the estimate. Appendix H.3 justifies the stop-gradient.

Finally, we expand log⁡pϕ​(y(i)∣x)=∑tlog⁡pϕ​(yt(i)∣x,y<t(i))\log p_{\phi}(y^{(i)}\mid x)=\sum_{t}\log p_{\phi}(y^{(i)}_{t}\mid x,y^{(i)}_{<t}), so that the loss is a sum over tokens. Dividing by T¯=1N​∑iTi\bar{T}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}T_{i} keeps the magnitude of the loss from growing with answer length, which would otherwise tie the effective learning rate to how long the answers are. The result is the sequence-level term of (9).

Appendix I The simplest case of the loss

Setting β=1\beta=1 reduces (8) to a sum of the log incremental importance weights of (2). Substituting the proposal qt∝pϕαq_{t}\propto p_{\phi}^{\alpha} and using log⁡Ztϕ=(1−α)​Hα​(pϕ)\log Z^{\phi}_{t}=(1-\alpha)H_{\alpha}(p_{\phi}),

logA~(i)=α[logpT(y(i)∣x)−logpϕ(y(i)∣x)]−(α−1)ℋ(i),ℋ(i)=∑tHα(pϕ(⋅∣x,y<t(i))).\log\tilde{A}^{(i)}=\alpha\Big[\log p_{\mathrm{T}}(y^{(i)}\mid x)-\log p_{\phi}(y^{(i)}\mid x)\Big]-(\alpha-1)\,\mathcal{H}^{(i)},\qquad\mathcal{H}^{(i)}=\sum_{t}H_{\alpha}\big(p_{\phi}(\cdot\mid x,y^{(i)}_{<t})\big).

At initialization in self-distillation the first bracket vanishes and A¯(i)=softmaxi​(−(α−1)​ℋ(i))\bar{A}^{(i)}=\mathrm{softmax}_{i}\!\left(-(\alpha-1)\mathcal{H}^{(i)}\right), a softmax over the negative total Rényi entropy along each answer, scaled by α−1\alpha-1. With λ=0\lambda=0 the loss is then maximum likelihood on the student’s own answers, each weighted by how confident the student was along it. As training proceeds, the first bracket becomes nonzero and shifts weight toward answers that the frozen teacher rates more highly than the current student does.

Appendix J Full experimental configuration

Models.

Qwen2.5-Math-7B (main, self-distillation), Qwen3-8B-Base, Qwen3-14B-Base, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, deepseek-math-7b-rl, and Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B as student with Qwen2.5-Math-7B as teacher for the λ\lambda sweep. In self-distillation teacher and student are initialized from the same checkpoint; the teacher is then frozen.

Sampler.

α=4\alpha=4, increased linearly from 11 over the first 20%20\% of training steps; N=16N=16 candidates; block length Δ=64\Delta=64; resampling when ESS<N/2\mathrm{ESS}<N/2; systematic resampling; β=0.7\beta=0.7; the proposal distribution is the student at temperature 1/α1/\alpha. The teacher’s next-token distributions are truncated to the top 6464 tokens and renormalized. The probability retained by the truncation is logged, and it exceeds 0.980.98 throughout except on the first block of unusually long prompts.

Optimization.

300300 steps, two prompts per step, learning rate 5×10−65\times 10^{-6} (3×10−63\times 10^{-6} for Qwen3-14B-Base and 1×10−51\times 10^{-5} for the Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B students) with 1010 warmup steps, no weight decay, gradient clipping at 1.01.0, 8-bit AdamW (Dettmers et al., 2022), gradient checkpointing, microbatch size 11 in the gradient phase, 10241024 generated tokens during training (20482048 for deepseek-math-7b-rl, whose answers are longer).

Evaluation.

Four samples per problem, 200200 problems each from GSM8K and MATH500, 20482048 generated tokens (30723072 for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and 40964096 for deepseek-math-7b-rl, whose answers are longer). We use the prompt builder, answer parser and grader of the reference power-sampling implementation so that our numbers are directly comparable with published measurements on the same models. Temperature-11 rows use each model’s own generation configuration, which is temperature 11 with no truncation for the Qwen models and temperature 0.60.6 with nucleus sampling at p=0.9p=0.9 for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Temperature-1/α1/\alpha rows set τ=0.25\tau=0.25 explicitly and keep the rest of that configuration, so Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is sampled there with nucleus sampling at p=0.9p=0.9.

Prompt formats.

Each model is trained and evaluated with the same prompt format. deepseek-math-7b-rl uses the instruction its model card specifies.

Training corpora.

GSM8K training-split questions throughout, except Appendix B.12, which uses 40004000 problem statements from OpenR1-Math-220k. In both cases only the question text is used. For the latter we remove any training prompt whose normalized form (lowercased, alphanumeric characters only, first 400400 characters) matches any evaluation problem, so no benchmark question appears in training.
