Appendix N Why the student at temperature 1 fails as a proposal

Section 3.3 states that using the student at temperature 11 as the proposal distribution makes the sampler fail. The second term of (6), (α−1)​log⁡pϕ​(yt)(\alpha-1)\log p_{\phi}(y_{t}), has a standard deviation of about 4.64.6 nats per token at α=4\alpha=4. Across a block of Δ=64\Delta=64 tokens, the spread between candidates is therefore about 4.6​64≈374.6\sqrt{64}\approx 37 nats, against a usable range of log⁡N=log⁡16≈2.8\log N=\log 16\approx 2.8 nats. With this proposal, ESS/N\mathrm{ESS}/N stays at 1/N1/N from the first block onward, which makes the sampler equivalent to selecting one candidate at random. The failure raises no error and produces no unusual value in the training log. The normalized importance weights are a softmax over the log importance weights, so a gap of 3535 nats between the two largest gives the second a relative weight of e−35≈6×10−16e^{-35}\approx 6\times 10^{-16}. Resampling then replaces all NN candidates with copies of one. From that point on, the candidates carry a single distinct answer and no longer approximate πα\pi_{\alpha}, and the estimator of Theorem 2 has a single sample. With the student at temperature 1/α1/\alpha as the proposal, this term cancels exactly, and the measured ESS/N\mathrm{ESS}/N during training lies between 0.390.39 and 0.640.64 for every model we train.

As a check on the algebra, setting the student equal to the teacher makes the teacher–student difference term vanish, so by Theorem 1 the incremental importance weights should be identical for every candidate. The measured ESS/N\mathrm{ESS}/N in this configuration is 0.9980.998.

Appendix O Implementation correctness

Several results concern distributions rather than accuracy, so we verify the implementation independently of any benchmark with fifty automated checks on small randomly initialized models, which run the same code as training.

  • •

    Theorem 2, and the exactness of holding the weights fixed, against brute-force enumeration and numerical differentiation: agreement to 10−1010^{-10} for β∈{0.25,0.5,1,2,5}\beta\in\{0.25,0.5,1,2,5\}.

  • •

    Log-probabilities recorded during generation and recomputed in the gradient step agree to 4.8×10−74.8\times 10^{-7} with resampling forced at every block. This tests token alignment and the reordering of the attention key-value cache for student and teacher.

  • •

    Loss and gradient match a direct reference implementation to 10−610^{-6} and 3×10−83\times 10^{-8}, and accumulating gradients over microbatches matches a single backward pass to 7×10−97\times 10^{-9}.

  • •

    The total variation distance between the sampler’s output distribution and πα\pi_{\alpha}, computed by exhaustive enumeration on a small model, decreases monotonically in NN (0.1660.166, 0.0950.095, 0.0650.065 at N=4,16,64N=4,16,64) against 0.1120.112 for the untrained model. This is the O⁡(1/N)O(1/N) behavior expected of a correct sampler.

  • •

    With the student equal to the teacher, Theorem 1 predicts equal weights, and the measured ESS/N\mathrm{ESS}/N is 0.9980.998 against a theoretical 1.0001.000.

These checks found three defects before any reported run: the amplification of training weights at resampling (Section 3.5), activation memory that grew with NN instead of with the microbatch size, and proposal log-probabilities that were discarded.

Appendix P Correcting the weight advantage of stopping early

Equation (5) implies that the log importance weight decreases at every token. A candidate that emits the end-of-sequence token keeps its weight fixed while unfinished candidates continue to lose weight, so stopping early gains weight for reasons unrelated to answer quality. For long chains of reasoning, this would train the model to stop reasoning early, and the loss curve would give no sign of it.

We charge each finished candidate the mean per-token increment in log importance weight of the unfinished ones. This is the same constant for every finished candidate at a given step, so the normalized weights among unfinished candidates are unchanged, and only the comparison between finished and unfinished candidates is corrected. As a diagnostic, we use the mean answer length weighted by the normalized importance weights minus the unweighted mean length, which should be near zero.

We measure this diagnostic in a controlled setting where student and teacher are the same model, so that the per-token decrease is identical across candidates and any preference for length comes from the weight accounting:

weighted minus unweighted length ESS/N\mathrm{ESS}/N
without the correction −25.9-25.9 tokens 0.0840.084
with the correction +0.13+0.13 tokens 0.9970.997

Appendix Q Resampling and the training weights

Resampling duplicates candidates. The training weights already recorded for earlier blocks are stored per candidate, so a duplicated candidate carries its ancestor’s recorded weight once per copy. Without a correction, the total training weight on an earlier block grows with every resampling step (a block that survives kk steps is amplified by up to NkN^{k}), and the opening tokens of every answer come to dominate the loss. Neither the loss value nor any standard diagnostic shows this.

Duplication is how resampling represents weight, so the recorded training weights must be renormalized to compensate. After each resampling step, we renormalize the stored training weights of every earlier block to sum to one across candidates. The test suite of Appendix O checks this property automatically.

The sampler and the loss also keep separate weight accumulators. The sampler’s accumulator uses (2) and decides when to resample. Replacing it with the training weight, which depends on β\beta, would stop the sampler from approximating πα\pi_{\alpha}. The loss accumulator uses (8), is reset at every block boundary, and supplies A¯(i)\bar{A}^{(i)}. Their per-token increments agree at β=1\beta=1, but for every β\beta they accumulate over different windows. We write the training weight with the letter AA to keep it distinct from the importance weight WW.
